## The question that started the analysis

What can a large public-health survey tell us about the relationship between everyday circumstances and mental health? I explored whether **household income, age, and physical activity** were associated with the number of days adults reported that their mental health was not good in the preceding month.

I approached this as an exploratory, observational analysis—not a test of whether any of these characteristics *cause* better or worse mental health. The goal was to find patterns, understand their size, and see how well a statistical model could summarize them.

## Data and approach

The data come from the **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)**, **2021 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS)**. The analysis uses a CSV subset of the survey containing 438,693 records before cleaning. The original source, survey documentation, and related resources are available on the [CDC's 2021 BRFSS annual data page](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2021.html).

I used **R and the tidyverse** to prepare the data, **ggplot2** to explore distributions and relationships, and **linear regression** to compare increasingly detailed models. The source CSV should be named `brfss2021.csv` and placed alongside this document to reproduce the analysis. The dataset is not embedded in this document.

## 1. Preparing the survey responses

I first examined the available variables and chose `MENTHLTH` as the outcome: the reported number of days in the last 30 when mental health was not good. The explanatory variables were `INCOME3` (household income category), `_AGE_G` (age group), and `EXERANY2` (whether the respondent reported exercise or physical activity).

The survey includes special response codes that cannot be treated as ordinary numbers. I removed refusals, don't-know responses, and missing values from the selected fields, then recoded `MENTHLTH = 88` (none) to **0 days**. Income remained an ordered 11-category variable, age an ordered six-group variable, and exercise a Yes/No factor. This produced **339,216 complete observations** for the analysis. Complete-case filtering makes the workflow straightforward but can introduce selection bias if excluded respondents differ systematically from included respondents.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(psych)
library(lm.beta)

brf <- read_csv("brfss2021.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) 
```

```{r}
Q11a <- brf %>%
  select(MENTHLTH, INCOME3, `_AGE_G`, EXERANY2) %>%
  arrange(MENTHLTH)
Q11a

Q11b <- Q11a %>%
  select(menthlth = MENTHLTH,
         income = INCOME3,
         age = `_AGE_G`,
         exercise = EXERANY2)
Q11b

Q11c <- Q11b %>%
  filter(!menthlth %in% c(77, 99)) %>%
  filter(!income %in% c(77, 99)) %>%
  filter(!exercise %in% c(7,9)) %>%
  drop_na(menthlth, income, age, exercise)

Q11 <- Q11c %>%
  mutate(
    menthlth = if_else(menthlth == 88, 0, menthlth),
    income = factor(income, levels = 1:11, ordered = TRUE),
    age = factor(age, levels = 1:6, ordered = TRUE),
    exercise = factor(exercise, levels = c(1, 2),
                      labels = c("Yes", "No")))
Q11

nrow(brf)
nrow(Q11)
```

## 2. Discovering the shape of the data

The first surprise was the distribution of poor mental-health days. **The median was zero, while the mean was approximately 4.21 days**. About **61.57%** of the cleaned responses reported zero poor mental-health days. This concentration at zero, combined with a smaller group reporting many poor days, created a strongly right-skewed distribution.

I visualized each variable separately and then compared mental-health days across income and exercise groups. The charts helped identify patterns that would be obscured by a single overall average.

```{r}
Q12_menthlth <- Q11 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = menthlth)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Poor Mental Health Days Distribution",
    x = "Past 30 Days Poor Mental Health",
    y = "Count"
  )
Q12_menthlth

Q12_income <- Q11 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = income)) + 
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Household Income",
    x = "Income Category", 
    y = "Count"
  )
Q12_income

Q12_age <- Q11 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title =  "Distribution of Age Groups",
    x = "Age Group",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = c("18-24", "25-34", "35-44", 
               "45-54", "55-64", "65+")
  )
Q12_age

Q12_exercise <- Q11 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = exercise)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Exercise",
    x = "Exercise",
    y = "Count"
  )
Q12_exercise

Q12_menthlth_exercise <- Q11 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = exercise, y = menthlth)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Poor Mental Health Days by Exercise",
    x = "Exercise",
    y = "Poor Mental Health Days"
  )
Q12_menthlth_exercise

Q12_menthlth_income <- Q11 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = income, y = menthlth)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Poor Mental Health Days by Income Category",
    x = "Income Category",
    y = "Poor Mental Health Days"
  )
Q12_menthlth_income

Q11 %>%
  group_by(income) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(menthlth),
    median = median(menthlth),
    Q1 = quantile(menthlth, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(menthlth, 0.75),
    min = min(menthlth),
    max = max(menthlth)
  )
```

## 3. Quantifying patterns—and deciding what counts as an outlier

Descriptive statistics added context to the plots. Respondents who reported exercising averaged **3.73** poor mental-health days, compared with **5.76** among those who did not. The mean also declined across income categories, from approximately **8.74 days** in the lowest category to **2.52 days** in the highest. These are group-level associations, not individual predictions or causal effects.

The age distribution was uneven: respondents aged **65 and older** made up approximately **33.33%** of the cleaned sample. I kept this imbalance in mind when interpreting the results.

Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, reports above **10 days** were flagged as statistical outliers: **45,543 records (13.43%)**. I chose **not to delete them**. Values from 0 to 30 are legitimate survey responses, and removing high values would disproportionately exclude people reporting more frequent mental-health difficulties. This choice preserves the outcome's real variation, although it makes ordinary linear regression assumptions harder to satisfy.

```{r}
Q13_menthlth <- Q11 %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(menthlth),
    median = median(menthlth),
    sd = sd(menthlth),
    variance = var(menthlth),
    Q1 = quantile(menthlth, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(menthlth, 0.75),
    IQR = IQR(menthlth),
    min = min(menthlth),
    max = max(menthlth)
  )
Q13_menthlth

Q13_income <- Q11 %>%
  count(income) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))
Q13_income
Q13_income_center <- Q11 %>%
  summarise(
    median_category = median(as.numeric(income)),
    modal_category = names(which.max(table(income)))
  )
Q13_income_center

Q13_income_spread <- Q11 %>%
  summarise(
    Q1 = quantile(as.numeric(income), 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(as.numeric(income), 0.75))
Q13_income_spread

Q13_age <- Q11 %>%
  count(age) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))
Q13_age

Q13_age_summary <- Q11 %>%
  summarise(
    median_age = median(as.numeric(age)),
    mode_age = names(which.max(table(age))),
    Q1 = quantile(as.numeric(age), 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(as.numeric(age), 0.75)
  )
Q13_age_summary

Q13_exercise <- Q11 %>%
  count(exercise) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))
Q13_exercise

Q13_menthlth_exercise <- Q11 %>%
  group_by(exercise) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(menthlth),
    median = median(menthlth),
    sd = sd(menthlth), 
    Q1 = quantile(menthlth, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(menthlth, 0.75),
    IQR = IQR(menthlth))
Q13_menthlth_exercise

Q13_methlth_income <- Q11 %>%
  group_by(income) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(menthlth),
    median = median(menthlth),
    sd = sd(menthlth),
    Q1 = quantile(menthlth, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(menthlth, 0.75),
    IQR = IQR(menthlth))
Q13_methlth_income

Q13_outliers <- Q11 %>%
  summarise(
    Q1 = quantile(menthlth, 0.25),
    Q3 = quantile(menthlth, 0.75),
    IQR = IQR(menthlth),
    lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR,
    upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR)
Q13_outliers

Q13_potential_outliers <- Q11 %>%
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    potential_outliers = 
      sum(menthlth > Q13_outliers$upper),
    percent_outliers =
      round(mean(menthlth > Q13_outliers$upper) * 100, 2)
  )
Q13_potential_outliers
```

## 4. Testing whether additional predictors improve the model

I built three nested linear regression models, adding information in stages:

1. **Income only**
2. **Income and exercise**
3. **Income, exercise, and age group**

To estimate a single income trend, I represented the ordered income categories by their category numbers. This is a modeling simplification: the categories do **not** represent equally spaced dollar amounts. In the third model, age was treated as a categorical predictor, allowing age groups to have different estimated effects rather than forcing a straight-line age trend.

| Model | Predictors | R² | Residual standard error |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| 1 | Income | 0.0284 | 8.08 days |
| 2 | Income + exercise | 0.0328 | 8.06 days |
| 3 | Income + exercise + age | **0.0683** | **7.91 days** |

Model 3 performed best **among the three models tested**, with the highest R² and lowest residual standard error and AIC. But it explained only **6.83%** of the variation in poor mental-health days. The improvement is meaningful as a comparison between these models, not evidence that the final model can predict any individual's mental health accurately.

The residual and Q–Q diagnostic plots also showed substantial departures from typical linear regression assumptions, consistent with the bounded, zero-heavy outcome. I therefore treated the regression primarily as a tool for exploring associations.

```{r}
Q14_model1 <- lm(menthlth ~ income, data = Q11)
summary(Q14_model1)

Q14_model1 <- Q11 %>%
  mutate(income_num = as.numeric(income)) %>%
  lm(menthlth ~ income_num, data = .)
summary(Q14_model1)

plot(Q14_model1, which = 1)

plot(Q14_model1, which = 2)

Q14_model2 <- Q11 %>%
  mutate(income_num = as.numeric(income)) %>%
  lm(menthlth ~ income_num + exercise, data = .)
summary(Q14_model2)

plot(Q14_model2, which = 1)

plot(Q14_model2, which = 2)

Q14_model3 <- Q11 %>%
  mutate(income_num = as.numeric(income)) %>%
  lm(menthlth ~ income_num + exercise + factor(age, ordered = FALSE), 
     data = .)
summary(Q14_model3)

plot(Q14_model3, which = 1)

plot(Q14_model3, which = 2)

Q14_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
  R_squared = c(
    summary(Q14_model1)$r.squared,
    summary(Q14_model2)$r.squared,
    summary(Q14_model3)$r.squared
  ),
Adjusted_R_Squared = c(
  summary(Q14_model1)$adj.r.squared,
  summary(Q14_model2)$adj.r.squared,
  summary(Q14_model3)$adj.r.squared
))
Q14_comparison

Q14_AIC <- AIC(
  Q14_model1,
  Q14_model2,
  Q14_model3
)

Q14_AIC

Q14_ANOVA <- anova(
  Q14_model1,
  Q14_model2,
  Q14_model3
)
Q14_ANOVA

Q14_RSE <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
  RSE = c(
    sigma(Q14_model1),
    sigma(Q14_model2),
    sigma(Q14_model3)
  )
)
Q14_RSE
```

## 5. Turning the model into illustrative predictions

To see what the fitted model implies for different combinations of characteristics, I constructed three hypothetical profiles. These are **illustrations of the model's estimated conditional mean**, not forecasts of a real person's future mental-health experience.

| Profile | Income category | Exercise | Age group | Predicted poor mental-health days (rounded) |
|:--|--:|:--|:--|--:|
| A | 3 | No | 25–34 | 9 |
| B | 7 | Yes | 35–44 | 5 |
| C | 11 | No | 65+ | 1 |

The third profile has a lower prediction despite reporting no exercise. That is not a contradiction: the model considers **income, exercise, and age together**. Because all three inputs differ between these profiles, the differences cannot be attributed to one predictor in isolation. Rounded whole-day values are for presentation; the underlying fitted estimates are continuous.

```{r}
Q15_individuals <- data.frame(
  income_num = c(3, 7, 11),
  exercise = factor(c("No", "Yes", "No"),
                    levels = levels(Q11$exercise)),
  age = factor(c(2, 3, 6), 
               levels = levels(Q11$age), 
               ordered = TRUE ))
Q15_individuals
Q15_predictions <- Q15_individuals %>%
  mutate(
    predicted_menthlth = round(predict(
      Q14_model3,
      newdata = Q15_individuals
    )
  ))
Q15_predictions
```

## What I learned

The strongest lesson from this project was that **finding a statistically detectable relationship is not the same as building a strong predictive model**. Income, physical activity, and age were associated with reported poor mental-health days in the survey, but most individual variation remained unexplained. Self-reported responses, broad income and age categories, a binary exercise measure, missing-data exclusions, and the unusual distribution of the outcome all limit interpretation.

This work strengthened my ability to move through an end-to-end analysis: define a research question, interpret a codebook, clean survey data, visualize distributions, make defensible outlier decisions, compare models, inspect diagnostics, and communicate results with appropriate caution. A future extension could test approaches better suited to bounded, zero-heavy count outcomes and account for the BRFSS survey design and weights.

## Source and reproducibility

**Data source:** Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, *Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), 2021 Annual Data*. [Official CDC source](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2021.html).

**Tools:** R, tidyverse/ggplot2, psych, and lm.beta. To reproduce the analysis, place an appropriately authorized copy of `brfss2021.csv` in the working directory and render this Quarto document in an R environment with the required packages installed. This case study is an independent portfolio presentation of the analysis and does not reproduce the course assignment instructions.
